sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Every Python fresher interview has at least one data structure question disguised as a problem-solving task: 'find duplicates', 'count frequencies', 'remove duplicates from a list'. The candidate who reaches for the right structure (set, dict, Counter) in 5 seconds looks far more capable than the one who writes a nested loop.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Pick the structure from the question requirement:

| Requirement | Structure |
|---|---|
| Ordered sequence, allows duplicates | `list` |
| Ordered, immutable, fixed data | `tuple` |
| Key→value lookup, O(1) access | `dict` |
| Unique elements, fast membership test | `set` |
| Ordered dict + unique | `dict` (insertion order since 3.7) |

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **list vs tuple** — both ordered and indexed, but tuple is immutable. Use tuple for data that shouldn't change (coordinates, RGB values).
- **dict lookup is O(1)** — because it's a hash table. List search is O(n).
- **set operations** — union (`|`), intersection (`&`), difference (`-`). Know these for 'common elements' interview problems.
- **Comprehensions** — `[x*2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]` is Pythonic and faster than an equivalent for-loop append.
- **`collections.Counter`** — frequency counting in one line. Many fresher problems are just frequency counts.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **'List vs tuple'** — mutability is the keyword. Then add 'tuple is slightly faster and can be used as a dict key'.
- **'How does Python dict work internally?'** — hash table with collision handling. Keys must be hashable (immutable).
- **'How do you remove duplicates from a list?'** — `list(set(my_list))` but loses order. `dict.fromkeys(my_list)` preserves order (Python 3.7+).
- **'When would you use a set over a list?'** — when you need O(1) membership test (`in` operator) and don't need order.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"When choosing a data structure I ask: do I need order? do I need duplicates? do I need fast lookup by key? List for ordered sequences, dict for key-value, set for unique fast-lookup. In this problem I'd reach for X because Y."*
